inline.s: [Again, the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitāyus Buddha, the towers and
guàn

railings — all are likewise naturally formed of the seven treasures, woven through with white pearls and mani gems, bright and wondrous beyond compare. The palaces and halls wherein the bodhisattvas dwell are likewise so.]

Again: the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitābha Buddha, the towers and railings — all are likewise naturally formed of the seven treasures, interwoven with white pearls and mani gems, bright and wondrous beyond compare. The palaces and halls in which the bodhisattvas dwell are likewise so.
[Towers and terraces (
guàn
)] A general term for tall buildings such as towers and halls. [Railings] Balustrades. “Lan” is a horizontal railing; “shun (
shǔn/dùn
)” is a vertical railing. [The seven treasures] Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, amber, fine jade, and carnelian. [Woven through] Interlaced.

[Among them are those who on the ground expound the sutras and those who recite them; those who on the ground receive the sutras and those who listen to them; those who on the ground walk in meditation, ponder the Way, and sit in Chan; and those in the sky who expound and recite, receive and listen, walk in meditation, ponder the Way, and sit in Chan.]

There, some on the ground expound the sutras and some recite them; some on the ground receive the sutras and some listen to them; some on the ground walk in meditation, ponder the Way, and sit in Chan; and some in the sky expound and recite, receive and listen, walk in meditation, ponder the Way, and sit in Chan.

[Some attain srota-āpanna, some sakṛdāgāmin, some anāgāmin, and some arhatship. Those who have not attained the stage of non-retrogression attain it. Each reflects on the Way, speaks of the Way, and practices the Way, all filled with joy.]

They attain the fruit of srota-āpanna, or of sakṛdāgāmin, or of anāgāmin and arhatship. Those who have not attained the stage of non-retrogression attain it. Each reflects on the Way, speaks of the Way, and practices the Way, all filled with joy.

[The four fruits] The four fruits of the śrāvaka vehicle, in order: the fruit of srota-āpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, and the fruit of arhatship. [Non-retrogression] That is, a-pi (
pí
) ba-zhi, meaning: no falling back. This is to say that one who reaches this stage advances only upward, step by step, until Buddhahood, with no regression in between.

blocks.text: 17. The Merit of Springs and Pools

inline.s: [Springs and pools] Flowing springs and bathing pools. The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha of the Tathāgata, Who Ferries Beings Across in the Human Realm (the Wu translation) says:

“In the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitābha Buddha, and in the dwellings of the bodhisattvas and arhats, within and without, in every place, there are likewise natural flowing springs and bathing pools.”

[In the lecture halls and monasteries, and in the dwellings of the bodhisattvas and arhats, within and without, in every place, there are natural flowing springs and bathing pools. Their water is limpid, fragrant, and clean, and possesses the eight excellent qualities: first, clear and pure; second, cool and refreshing; third, sweet and delicious; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening and nourishing; sixth, calm and harmonious; seventh, when drunk, it removes hunger, thirst, and immeasurable other afflictions; eighth, once drunk, it surely nourishes the faculties and the four great elements and increases all manner of supreme good roots.]

In the lecture halls and monasteries, and in the dwellings of the bodhisattvas and arhats, within and without, in every place, there are natural flowing springs and bathing pools. Their water is limpid, fragrant, and clean, and possesses eight excellent qualities:

first, clear and pure; second, cool and refreshing; third, sweet and delicious; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening and nourishing; sixth, calm and harmonious; seventh, when drunk, it removes hunger, thirst, and immeasurable other afflictions; eighth, once drunk, it surely nourishes body and mind and increases all manner of supreme good roots.
[Limpid] Clear and bright. [Possessing the eight excellent qualities] The Sūtra of Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha's Reception says:

“In the pure Buddha-land of Ultimate Bliss, in every place there are pools of seven wondrous treasures, filled to the brim with water of eight excellent qualities. What are these eight excellent qualities called? First, clear and pure; second, cool and refreshing; third, sweet and delicious; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening and nourishing; sixth, calm and harmonious; seventh, when drunk, it removes hunger, thirst, and immeasurable other afflictions; eighth, once drunk, it surely nourishes the faculties and the four great elements and increases all manner of supreme good roots.”

[The faculties and the four great elements] This refers to body and mind. “The faculties” are the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. “The four great elements” are earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has the nature of solidity, water of moisture, fire of warmth, wind of motion. All tangible things in the world (including the body) possess these four natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, and so they are called “great.”
When the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to bathe, each enters his own pool of seven treasures to bathe.

Those who wish the water to reach their feet, to reach their knees, to reach their waists and armpits, to reach their necks, or who wish it to wash over their bodies, or who wish it cold, warm, swift, or slow — the water in each case follows the minds of those beings, opening the spirit and gladdening the body. Pure as though formless, with jeweled sands shining through, there is no depth it does not illumine. Gentle ripples slowly turn, pouring into one another.]

When the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to bathe, each enters his own pool of seven treasures to bathe. Those who wish the water to reach their feet, their knees, their waists, their armpits, or their necks, or who wish the pool water to shower over their bodies of itself, or who wish it cold, warm, swift, or slow — the water follows each of their minds in every case. Moreover, it makes the bather's spirit clear and bright and his body glad and at ease. The pool water is clear and formless, the seven treasures and the golden sands reflecting one another, and there is no depth it does not illumine. Gentle ripples (small waves) slowly turn, pouring into one another.
The Assembly of the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life (the Tang translation) says:

“When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, together with the bodhisattvas and arhats, wishes to bathe, each enters his own pool of seven treasures to bathe. If a bodhisattva or arhat wishes the water to cover his feet, the water covers his feet. If he wishes it to reach his knees, it reaches his knees. If he wishes it to reach his waist, it reaches his waist. If he wishes it to reach his armpits, it reaches his armpits. If he wishes it to reach his neck, it reaches his neck. If he wishes it to wash over his body, it washes over his body. If he wishes the water to return to its former state, it returns to its former state. It is as free and as pleasing as one could wish.”

[Amitābha Buddha's jeweled pool is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. All is formed in turn by the seven treasures, mutually completing one another. The sand at its bottom is all seven-treasure white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls.]

Amitābha Buddha's pool of seven treasures is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. All is formed in turn by the seven treasures, mutually completing one another. The sand at its bottom is all seven-treasure white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls.
[Amitābha Buddha's bathing pool] The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, Equality, and Enlightenment (the Han translation) says:

“The Buddha said: ‘The bathing pool of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. Its bathing pool is entirely formed by the seven treasures turning and completing one another. The sand at the bottom of its water is likewise all seven-treasure white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls. The water in the bathing pool of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity and of the bodhisattvas and arhats is all pure, fragrant, and clean. In it there are always fragrant flowers — a hundred kinds of flowers all naturally growing, of many different colors and scents, each flower with a thousand petals, and all these flowers are fragrant beyond compare, a fragrance beyond words. The fragrance of these flowers is not that of worldly flowers, and surpasses even the flowers of heaven. The fragrance of these flowers is the essence of all flower fragrances in the eight directions, above and below, and arises naturally. The water in the pool flows and pours into itself in turn. The pool's water flows neither slowly nor swiftly, and of itself produces the five tones.’ The Buddha said: ‘In the countless Buddha-lands in the eight directions, above and below, the gods and humans and the winged and crawling creatures — all who are born in the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity are born by transformation in the lotus flowers of this water of seven treasures.’”
[The sand at its bottom is all seven-treasure white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls]
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha of the Tathāgata, Who Ferries Beings Across in the Human Realm (the Wu translation) says:

“The Buddha said: ‘The bathing pool of Amitābha Buddha is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. Its pool is entirely formed by the seven treasures turning and completing one another, and the sand at the bottom of its water is white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls.’”

[On the banks are candana (sandalwood) trees, auspicious-fruit trees, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers; their flowers and fruits are forever fragrant, their light shining brightly. Long branches and dense leaves interweave above the water, giving forth all manner of fragrance, which nothing in the world can compare. They scatter their fragrance on the wind
fù
, meaning fragrance)
, and along the flowing water they spread their scent.]

On the banks are candana trees, auspicious-fruit trees, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers; their flowers and fruits are forever fragrant, shining with light. Slender branches and dense leaves interweave above the water, giving forth all manner of wondrous fragrance, which nothing in the world can compare. Their fragrance scatters on the wind and spreads along the flowing water.

[The waves send forth immeasurable subtle and wondrous sounds: one hears the sounds of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; the sound of the pāramitās; the sound of stillness and quietude; the sound of non-arising and non-ceasing; the sound of the ten powers and the fearlessnesses; or one hears the sound of no-nature, no-activity, and no-self; the sound of great loving-kindness, great compassion, joy, and equanimity; the sound of the sweet dew of consecration and the receiving of the stage. Having heard all such sounds, one's mind becomes pure, free of all discrimination, upright, and equal, and one's good roots ripen. According to what one hears, one corresponds with the Dharma. Those who wish to hear it hear it alone; those who do not wish to hear it hear nothing at all. Never do they fall back from the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.]

The waves send forth immeasurable subtle and wondrous sounds: one hears the sound of the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha), the sound of the pāramitās, the sound of stillness and quietude, the sound of non-arising and non-ceasing, the sound of the ten powers and the fearlessnesses; or one hears the sound of no-nature, no-activity, and no-self, the sound of great loving-kindness, great compassion, joy, and equanimity, the sound of the sweet dew of consecration and the receiving of the stage. Having heard all such sounds, one's mind becomes pure, free of all discrimination, upright, and equal, and one's good roots ripen. According to the Dharma one hears, body and mind at once correspond with it. Those who wish to hear it hear it alone; those who do not wish to hear it hear nothing at all (not a single sound). Never do they fall back from the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

[The ten powers] The ten kinds of power possessed by the Tathāgata: 1. The power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible — the power to know the reasonableness and unreasonableness of all things; 2. The power of knowing the karmic retribution of the three times — the power to know the causal retribution throughout the three times of all sentient beings; 3. The power of knowing all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis — the power to know the various meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis; 4. The power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties — the power to know the superiority or inferiority of beings' faculties and the greatness or smallness of the fruits they attain; 5. The power of knowing all manner of understandings — the power to know universally the different realms of all beings; 6. The power of knowing all manner of realms — the power to know universally the different realms of all beings; 7. The power of knowing the paths that lead everywhere — the power to know the causes and effects of the paths practiced by all beings; 8. The power of the unobstructed divine eye — the power to see with the divine eye the birth and death of beings and the conditions of their good and evil karma without obstruction; 9. The power of the undefiled knowledge of past lives — the power to know beings' past lives and to know the undefiled nirvāṇa; 10. The power of knowing the eternal cutting off of habitual tendencies — the power to know truly that the residual habits of all deluded thoughts are forever cut off and no longer arise.

[No-activity] That which is without cause or condition, without fabrication. [No-self] The absence of the grasping at a personal self and the grasping at a dharma-self. The grasping at a personal self is not understanding the principle that the five aggregates are falsely combined, and deludedly grasping body and mind as a single, real self; the grasping at a dharma-self is not understanding the principle that all dharmas arise from conditions and are empty by nature, and deludedly grasping all dharmas as having a real essence and function. The Diamond Sūtra says:
“Those who comprehend the Dharma of no-self, the Tathāgata names true bodhisattvas.”

[Arising by conditions and empty by nature] “Arising by conditions” means that all things in the world arise from the coming together of many conditions; “empty by nature” means that the dharmas formed by the coming together of many conditions are empty in their own nature, without any real self-essence.

[All those reborn from the worlds of the ten directions are naturally born by transformation within the lotus flowers of these seven-treasure pools. All receive bodies of pure emptiness and the substance of the infinite. They do not hear even the names of the evil afflictions and sufferings of the three evil paths. Since the names do not exist, how much less the actual suffering? They hear only the sounds of natural joy and happiness. Therefore that land is named Ultimate Bliss.]

All those reborn from the worlds of the ten directions are naturally born by transformation within the lotus flowers of these seven-treasure pools. They all receive bodies of pure emptiness and the substance of the infinite. They do not hear even the names of the evil afflictions and sufferings of the three evil paths. Since even the names do not exist, how much less the actual suffering? They hear only the sounds of natural joy and happiness. Therefore that land is named Ultimate Bliss.
[A body of pure emptiness, the substance of the infinite] This is intertextual phrasing, meaning:
a body of pure emptiness and the infinite

. Not nourished by food and drink, it is called pure and empty; not destroyed by old age and death, it is called infinite. [Intertextual phrasing] Also called mutual phrasing, it is a rhetorical device often used in classical Chinese. Its characteristic is that it is neither wordy nor repetitious nor flatly narrated, but reserved and concise, sparing in words yet preserving the meaning, the two parts completing each other's sense and reflecting each other's brilliance. For example, in “The Ballad of Mulan,” “the generals fought a hundred battles and died, the warriors returned after ten years,” means: the generals and warriors fought a hundred battles and died, the generals and warriors returned after ten years. Again, for example, in “Record of Yueyang Tower,” “not rejoicing in things, not grieving in oneself” means: not rejoicing because of things or of oneself, and also not grieving because of things or of oneself. Here “things” refers to people other than oneself and to the circumstances in which one finds oneself, and “oneself” refers to one's own personal fortunes.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha of the Tathāgata, Who Ferries Beings Across in the Human Realm (the Wu translation) says:

“The Buddha said: ‘The bathing pool of Amitābha Buddha is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. Its pool is entirely formed by the seven treasures turning and completing one another, and the sand at the bottom of its water is white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls. The water in the bathing pool of Amitābha Buddha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats is all pure, fragrant, and clean. In the pool there are always fragrant flowers — a hundred kinds of flowers all naturally growing, of many different colors, each color and fragrance distinct. The branches all have a thousand petals, and are fragrant beyond compare, a fragrance beyond words. These flowers are not worldly flowers, nor are they flowers of heaven. The fragrance of these flowers is the essence of all flower fragrances in the eight directions, above and below, and arises by transformation of itself. The water in the pool flows and pours into itself in turn. Its water flows neither slowly nor swiftly
(kuài, in ancient usage interchangeable with “fast”)

, and of itself produces the five tones.’ The Buddha said: ‘In the countless Buddha-lands in the eight directions, above and below, the gods and humans and the winged and crawling creatures — all who are born in the land of Amitābha Buddha — are all born by transformation in the lotus flowers of the water of seven treasures. They then naturally grow up, and there is none who suckles them; they all eat naturally provided food and drink. Their bodies are neither the bodies of worldly humans nor the bodies of heavenly beings. All have accumulated the virtue of many good deeds, and all receive naturally the body of emptiness and the substance of the infinite, and are beautiful and lovely beyond compare.’”

[In that land of Ultimate Bliss, all sentient beings are of surpassing and wondrous countenance, rare in the world. They are all of one kind, without marks of difference. Only because they accord with the customs of other lands are they called gods and humans.]

In the land of Ultimate Bliss, all sentient beings have countenances and complexions that are exceedingly subtle and wondrous, rare in the world. They are all entirely of one kind, with no difference of better or worse. Only because they accord with the customs of other worlds are they called gods and humans.
[All] All, entirely.

[The Buddha told Ānanda: Suppose a poor beggar of the world stood beside an emperor — could their faces and forms be considered alike? If the emperor were compared with a wheel-turning sage king, he would be coarse and base, just as the beggar beside the emperor. The wheel-turning sage king is foremost in majestic appearance, yet compared with the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven he is again ugly and inferior. Suppose the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven were compared with the king of the sixth heaven: they are not alike even a hundred thousand times over. And if the king of the sixth heaven were compared with the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas in the land of Ultimate Bliss, in the radiance of their countenances and complexions, they would not come within even a trillion times.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: Suppose a poor beggar of the world stood beside an emperor — could their faces and forms be of one kind? If the emperor were compared with a wheel-turning sage king, he would be coarse and ugly, just as the beggar beside the emperor. The wheel-turning sage king is foremost in majestic appearance, yet compared with the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven he appears ugly and inferior. Suppose the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven (Indra) were compared with the king of the sixth heaven (the king of Paranirmita-vaśavartin): the difference is far more than a hundred thousand times. And if the king of the sixth heaven were compared with the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas in the land of Ultimate Bliss, in the radiance of their countenances and complexions, the difference is far more than a trillion times
[The sixth heaven] The heaven of desire has six levels in all; Paranirmita-vaśavartin, the heaven of the enjoyment of others' emanations, is the sixth, and so it is called “the sixth heaven.”

[Their palaces, clothing, food, and drink are like those of the king of Paranirmita-vaśavartin. As for their majesty and virtue, their stages, and their spiritual penetrations and transformations, all gods and humans cannot be compared with them — by a hundred thousand million times, incalculably many times, they cannot be matched.]

All sentient beings in the land of Ultimate Bliss have palaces, clothing, food, and drink like those of the king of Paranirmita-vaśavartin. As for majesty and virtue, stages, and spiritual penetrations and transformations, all gods and humans of other worlds cannot be compared with them; the difference is far more than a hundred thousand million times, beyond all reckoning.
[Ānanda, you should know that the land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha is adorned with such merit and virtue — inconceivable!]
Ānanda, you should know that the land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha is adorned with such merit and virtue — inconceivable!

[Moreover, all sentient beings in the land of Ultimate Bliss — whether already born there, now being born there, or to be born there — all obtain such wondrous bodies of form. Their forms are dignified and imposing, their blessings and virtue immeasurable. Their wisdom is clear and bright, their spiritual penetrations free and unimpeded. They enjoy all manner of things, everything in abundance. Palaces, clothing and adornments, fragrant flowers, banners, and canopies, and the implements of adornment — whatever they need at will, all is as they think of it.]

Moreover, all sentient beings in the land of Ultimate Bliss — whether already born there (or those who have already been born there), now being born there (or those now being born there), or to be born there (or those who will be born there) — all obtain such wondrous bodies of form. Their forms are dignified and imposing, their blessings and virtue immeasurable. Their wisdom is clear and bright, their spiritual penetrations free and unimpeded. They enjoy all manner of things, everything in abundance. Palaces, clothing and adornments, fragrant flowers, banners, and canopies, and the implements of adornment — whatever they need at will, all is exactly as they think of it.

[When they wish to eat, vessels of seven treasures appear of themselves before them, and food and drink of a hundred flavors of themselves fill them full. Though such food exists, in truth there is no one who eats it. They need only see its color and smell its fragrance, and are nourished by intention; their complexion and strength increase, yet there is no excretion. Body and mind are soft and gentle, with no attachment to any taste. When the meal is done it vanishes by transformation, and when the time comes it appears again.]

When they wish to eat, vessels of seven treasures of themselves appear before them, and food and drink of a hundred flavors of themselves fill them full. Though there is such fine food, it is not eaten into the belly. They need only see its color and smell its fragrance, and are nourished by intention; at once their complexion and strength increase, yet there is no excretion. Body and mind are soft and gentle, with no greed or attachment. When the meal is finished, the vessels of seven treasures of themselves vanish; when they wish to eat again, they are again filled with food and drink of a hundred flavors, appearing of themselves.
[There are also wondrous garments made of many treasures, crowns and sashes and necklaces, with immeasurable light and a hundred thousand wondrous colors, all complete and naturally upon the body.]

There are also wondrous garments made of many treasures, crowns, sashes, and necklaces; they are immeasurable in light and of a hundred thousand wondrous colors, all complete, and each according to the mind's wish naturally clothes the body.

[The dwellings in which they live accord with their forms and colors. Jeweled nets spread over them, and jeweled bells hang everywhere. Wondrous and rare treasures adorn them on every side. Their light and color blaze and shine, utterly magnificent and beautiful. Towers and railings, halls and chambers, wide or narrow, square or round, large or small, some in the sky, some on the ground. Pure, peaceful, and stable, subtly wondrous and joyful. At a thought they appear before one, and nothing is lacking.]

In the land of Ultimate Bliss, the dwellings of all sentient beings — their shapes and colors are entirely as their hearts desire. Jeweled nets cover them, and jeweled bells of every kind hang there. Wondrous and rare treasures adorn them on every side. Their light and color blaze and shine, utterly magnificent and beautiful. Towers and railings, halls and chambers, wide or narrow, square or round, large or small, some in the sky, some on the ground. Pure, peaceful, and stable, subtly wondrous and joyful. At their thought they appear before them, and nothing is lacking.
[Adornment] Decoration.

[In that Buddha-land, at every mealtime a virtuous wind naturally rises gently, blowing upon the nets and the host of jeweled trees, giving forth subtle and wondrous sounds that proclaim the pāramitās of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no-self, and spreading ten thousand kinds of gentle and elegant virtuous fragrance. Those who hear it find that the dust of affliction and the stains of habit naturally do not arise. When the wind touches their bodies, they are peaceful, harmonious, and well attuned, like a bhikṣu who has attained the concentration of extinction.]

In the land of Ultimate Bliss, at every mealtime a virtuous wind naturally rises gently, blowing upon the nets and the host of jeweled trees, giving forth subtle and wondrous sounds that proclaim the pāramitās of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no-self, and spreading ten thousand kinds of gentle and elegant virtuous fragrance. All who hear it find that their afflictions (the dust of toil) and evil habits (the stains of habit) naturally do not arise. When the wind touches their bodies, they are peaceful, harmonious, and well attuned, like a bhikṣu who has attained the concentration of extinction.
[Virtuous wind]

The pure breeze of the land of Ultimate Bliss, complete in ten thousand virtues. [Suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and no-self] Suffering means that this brief human life has three kinds of suffering, eight kinds of suffering, and immeasurable sufferings; emptiness is arising by conditions and emptiness by nature — arising by conditions means that all dharmas in the world arise from the coming together of many conditions, and emptiness by nature means that the dharmas formed by the coming together of many conditions are empty in their own nature, without a real self-essence; impermanence means that all formations are impermanent — all dharmas in the world change without cease, arising and ceasing without interruption, with no permanent, unchanging individual; no-self means that the person falsely formed by the five aggregates has no real, unchanging self-essence to be obtained. [The five aggregates] The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness — the five great elements that constitute the human person. [The concentration of extinction] Also called the concentration of the extinction of feeling and perception; this is the meditative concentration in which the six consciousnesses and their mental factors are extinguished and no longer arise. [Mental factors] The abbreviation of dharmas belonging to the mind, that is, the various psychological phenomena that belong to the mind.

[It again blows upon the jeweled groves and trees, and the drifting flowers gather into heaps, of many colors and lights, filling the Buddha-land. They arrange themselves in order according to their colors, without confusion. Soft, bright, and clean, like tūla cotton. When the foot treads upon them, they sink four fingers deep. When the foot is lifted, they return to their former state. After mealtime has passed, the flowers of themselves disappear, and the great earth is pure. New flowers rain down again, and in accordance with the seasons they again cover all, no different from before. Thus it happens six times.]

The virtuous wind again blows upon the jeweled groves and trees, and the drifting flowers gather into heaps (like a flowered terrace), flashing with many colors and lights, filling the Buddha-land. They arrange themselves in order according to their colors, without the least confusion. These fresh flowers are soft, bright, and clean, like tūla cotton; if the foot treads upon them, they sink three inches (four fingers wide); when the foot is lifted, they return to their former state. After mealtime, these flowers of themselves disappear, and the great earth is pure. In accordance with the seasons (morning, midday, sunset, first watch, middle watch, and last watch), new flowers rain down again and again, covering the Buddha-land. Six times each day, and so it is each time.
[Tūla cotton] The cotton produced by the tūla tree, like willow catkins.

[Again, lotuses of many treasures fill the whole world. Each jeweled flower has a hundred thousand kotis of petals. The light of these flowers is of immeasurable kinds and colors. Blue flowers emit blue light, white flowers emit white light; dark, yellow, vermilion, and purple, their light and color are likewise. There are also immeasurable wondrous treasures and a hundred thousand mani gems, adorning and embellishing the rare and wondrous, outshining the sun and moon.]

Again, lotuses of many treasures fill the whole land of Ultimate Bliss. Each jeweled flower has a hundred thousand kotis of petals. These jeweled lotuses radiate light of immeasurably many kinds and colors. Blue flowers emit blue light, white flowers emit white light; the light and color of dark (black), yellow, vermilion (red), and purple are likewise so. There are also immeasurable wondrous treasures and a hundred thousand mani gems, adorning and embellishing the rare and wondrous, outshining the sun and moon.

[The size of those lotuses is either half a yojana, or one, two, three, or four, up to a hundred thousand yojanas. From each flower issue thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of rays of light. Within each ray of light appear thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of Buddhas, their bodies the color of purple gold, their marks and excellences surpassing and rare. Each of these Buddhas again emits a hundred thousand rays of light and, universally throughout the ten directions, speaks the subtle Dharma. Thus do all these Buddhas each establish immeasurable sentient beings in the right Way of the Buddha.]

The diameter of those jeweled lotuses is either half a yojana, or one, or two, or three, or four yojanas, up to a hundred thousand yojanas. From each flower radiate thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of rays of light. Within each ray of light appear thirty-six hundred thousand kotis of Buddhas, their bodies the color of purple gold, their marks and excellences surpassing and rare. Each Buddha again emits a hundred thousand rays of light and, universally throughout the ten directions, expounds the subtle Dharma. Thus do all these Buddhas each establish immeasurable sentient beings in the right Way of the Buddha.

blocks.text: 22. Decisive Attainment of the Ultimate Fruit

inline.s: [Decisive attainment of the ultimate fruit] All sentient beings in the land of Ultimate Bliss will certainly become Buddhas.

[Moreover, Ānanda, in that Buddha-land there are no appearances of darkness, firelight, sun, moon, stars, or day and night, nor any names of years, months, or kalpas, nor any dwelling attached to family households. In every place there are neither markers nor names, nor any discrimination of taking and rejecting; they receive only purity and the highest joy.]

Moreover, Ānanda, in the land of Ultimate Bliss there are no appearances of darkness, firelight, sun, moon, stars, or day and night, nor any names of years, months, or kalpas, and still less any dwelling in family households as in this world. In every place there are neither names of streets, districts, or towns, nor any discrimination of taking and rejecting, of good and bad, fair and ugly; they receive only purity and the highest joy.
[Yao (
yào
)] The sun, moon, and stars are all called “yao.” For example, the sun, moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn are together called the “seven luminaries.”
[Still less]
In the text three “no” expressions come in succession (“
there are no
appearances of darkness, firelight, sun, moon, stars, or day and night,
nor any
names of years, months, or kalpas,
nor any
dwelling attached to family households”). Therefore “nor any” is rendered as “still less.”

[If good men or good women, whether already born there or to be born there, all dwell in the right and certain state, they will certainly realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Why? Because those in the wrong and certain state, and in the undetermined state, cannot understand the causes that establish that state.]

If good men or good women, whether already reborn in the land of Ultimate Bliss or to be reborn there in the future, as soon as they are reborn there all dwell in the right and certain state and will certainly become Buddhas (certainly realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi). Why? Because those who dwell in the wrong and certain state and in the undetermined state cannot understand how to create (establish) the causes of Buddhahood.
[If good men or good women, whether already born or to be born, all dwell in the right and certain state] The earlier text (“Vow 29: Abiding in the Right and Certain State”) says:
“When I attain Buddhahood, there shall be no evil names in my land. All sentient beings born in my land shall be of one mind and dwell in the certain state
(the right and certain state)

blocks.text: 23. Praises of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions

inline.s: [Moreover, Ānanda, in the worlds of the east, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in each world the Buddhas, numerous as those sands, each extend the mark of the broad and long tongue, emit immeasurable light, and speak words of truth, praising the inconceivable merit and virtue of Amitāyus Buddha. In the worlds of the south, west, and north, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the praises of the Buddhas are likewise so. In the worlds of the four intermediate directions and of above and below, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the praises of the Buddhas are likewise so.]

Moreover, Ānanda, in the worlds of the east, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in each world the Buddhas, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each extend the mark of the broad and long tongue, emit immeasurable light, and speak words of truth, praising the inconceivable merit and virtue of Amitābha Buddha. The Buddhas of the worlds of the south, west, and north, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, likewise praise him in this way. The Buddhas of the worlds of the four intermediate directions (southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast) and of above and below, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, likewise praise him in this way.

[The broad and long tongue] One of the thirty-two marks of a Buddha. The Buddha's tongue is broad and long, and moreover soft, red, and thin, able to cover his face up to the hairline. Since the mark of the tongue is thus, his words must be true.

[Why is this? Because they wish all sentient beings of other directions, hearing the name of that Buddha, to give rise to a pure mind, to recollect, receive, and uphold it, and to take refuge and make offerings. Even those able to give rise to a single thought of pure faith, dedicating all their good roots with sincere hearts and vowing to be born in that land — according to their vows they all attain birth, gain non-retrogression, and reach supreme, right, and equal enlightenment.]

Why do the Buddhas of the ten directions praise him in this way? It is to cause all sentient beings in the worlds of other directions, hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, to give rise to a pure mind, to recollect, receive, and uphold it, and to take refuge and make offerings. Even those able to give rise to a single thought (undefiled by stray thoughts) of pure faith, dedicating all their good roots with sincere hearts, vowing to be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss — according to their vows they all attain birth, gain the stage of non-retrogression (never falling back again), and reach Buddhahood.

[A single thought] A single, undivided thought (undefiled by deluded thoughts). The “single thought” here does not mean an extremely short moment (the snap of a finger) or a single occurrence of a thought.
The key to rebirth in the three grades: give rise to the bodhi mind and single-mindedly and exclusively recite.

[Giving rise to the bodhi mind] Giving rise to the great mind that seeks the Buddha-way above (perfect enlightenment and Buddhahood) and delivers sentient beings below. [Single-minded and exclusive recitation]
always reciting the Buddha's name with one mind, without any other thoughts
(for details see the
Single-Minded Exclusive Recitation
article
Concerning single-minded and exclusive recitation, Master Shandao — Amitābha Buddha come again — taught as follows:
When mindfulness continues, one is reborn at once
. If one can
keep thought following thought without a break
taking the whole of one's life as the term
— for such a person
, ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.
May all people reflect well: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one must
rouse the mind and restrain oneself
never let up day or night
, and when the former thought ends in death, the next thought is born at once.
Forever enjoying the dharma-bliss of the unconditioned, until Buddhahood — how joyful!

[Continuity brings rebirth] At the moment of death, one need only keep the thought of Buddha-recitation continuous (not interrupted by deluded thoughts) to attain rebirth in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss. [If one can keep thought following thought without a break, taking the whole of one's life as the term, ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn] If one can keep the thought of Buddha-recitation continuous and practices thus for a lifetime (
that is, one who recites single-mindedly and exclusively

), then where there are ten people, ten are reborn; where there are a hundred, a hundred are reborn. [Rousing the mind and restraining oneself] “Rousing the mind” means rousing one's mind to do what should be done; “restraining oneself” means restraining oneself from doing what should not be done. The four words “rouse the mind and restrain oneself” are a powerful weapon for overcoming difficulties and sweeping away obstacles. [Never let up day or night] Do not stop the unbroken succession of thoughts day or night. [When the former thought ends in death, the next thought is born] This means: because the thoughts of Buddha-recitation are continuous, the last thought at the moment of death is certainly a thought of Buddha-recitation, and immediately after that last thought one is reborn at once in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss.
(For details see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
[The Buddha told Ānanda: In the worlds of the ten directions, among the gods and humans, those who with sincere hearts wish to be born in that land fall into three grades.]
The Buddha told Ānanda: In the worlds of the ten directions, among the gods and humans,
those of sincere heart
(the most sincere and earnest) who wish to be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss fall into three grades (three classes).
The Sūtra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:
“The Buddha told Ānanda: In the worlds of the ten directions, among the gods and humans, those who with sincere hearts wish to be born in that land fall into three grades.”
[Those of the highest grade abandon the household, cast off desire, and become śramaṇas.
They give rise to the bodhi mind and single-mindedly and exclusively recite Amitābha Buddha.

They cultivate all merits and virtues and vow to be born in that land. When such sentient beings approach the end of their lives, Amitābha Buddha, together with all the hosts of sages, appears before them. In a moment, they follow that Buddha and are reborn in his land. There, within a lotus of seven treasures, they are naturally born by transformation, wise and courageous, with spiritual penetrations and freedom. Therefore, Ānanda, if sentient beings wish to see Amitābha Buddha in this present life, they should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi, and further should single-mindedly recollect the land of Ultimate Bliss, accumulate and gather good roots, and uphold and dedicate them. By this they see the Buddha and are born in that land, gain non-retrogression, and reach supreme bodhi.]

Those of the highest grade (the highest class): they abandon the household and cast off desire, shave their heads and become monks. They give rise to the bodhi mind and single-mindedly and exclusively recite Amitābha Buddha. They cultivate all merits and virtues and vow to be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss. When such sentient beings approach the end of their lives, Amitābha Buddha, together with all the hosts of sages, appears before them. In an instant, they follow that Buddha and are reborn in his land. There, within a lotus of seven treasures, they are naturally born by transformation, wise and courageous, with spiritual penetrations and freedom. Therefore, Ānanda, if sentient beings wish to see Amitābha Buddha in this present life, they should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi, and further should single-mindedly recollect the land of Ultimate Bliss, accumulate and gather good roots, and uphold and dedicate them. By this they see the Buddha and are born in that land, gain the stage of non-retrogression, and reach Buddhahood.
[Dedicating as one should] One should take this merit and dedicate it:
“By this merit, may the Buddha's Pure Land be adorned
(the Western land of Ultimate Bliss)
, repaying the four kinds of kindness above and relieving the three evil paths below
(the three evil destinies)
of suffering, and may all who see or hear this give rise to the bodhi mind; when this one retribution body ends, be born together in the land of Ultimate Bliss.”

[The four kinds of kindness] The kindness of parents (the family), the kindness of sentient beings (society), the kindness of the land (the nation), and the kindness of the Three Jewels (religion). [The Three Jewels] The Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Sangha. [When this one retribution body ends, be born together in the land of Ultimate Bliss] This means that all, at the end of this present life, are reborn in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss. Here “retribution body” means the body of karmic retribution.
[Those of the middle grade, though unable to become śramaṇas and greatly cultivate merit and virtue,
should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively recite Amitābha Buddha

. According to their own capacity they cultivate all good merits and virtues, uphold the fasts and precepts, erect stupas and images, feed śramaṇas, hang silk banners and light lamps, scatter flowers and burn incense, and with this dedicate themselves, vowing to be born in that land. When such a person is about to die, Amitābha Buddha manifests a transformed body, whose light and marks and excellences are fully like the true Buddha, and together with a great multitude, surrounding him before and behind, appears before that person, receiving and guiding him. At once, following the transformed Buddha, he is born in that land, dwells in non-retrogression, and reaches supreme bodhi. His merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the highest grade.]

Those of the middle grade (the middle class): though unable to shave their heads and leave home and greatly cultivate merit and virtue, they should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively recite Amitābha Buddha. According to their own capacity they cultivate all good merits and virtues, uphold the fasts and precepts, build stupas, temples, and Buddha images, give alms to monks and nuns, and make offerings to the Buddha by hanging silk banners, lighting lamps, scattering flowers, and burning incense, and with this they dedicate themselves, vowing to be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss. When such a person is about to die, Amitābha Buddha manifests a transformed body, whose light, marks, and excellences are entirely like the true Buddha, and together with a great multitude surrounding him before and behind, appears before that person, receiving and guiding him. At once, following the transformed Buddha, he is born in that land, dwells in the stage of non-retrogression, and reaches Buddhahood. His merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the highest grade.

[The fasts and precepts] Cleansing the impurities of one's own mind is called “the fast”; prohibiting the faults of one's own conduct is called “the precepts.” The fasts and precepts mean keeping the precepts so as to cut off all craving and all faults. [Zeng (
zēng
)] The general term in ancient times for silk fabrics. [Hanging silk banners] Hanging banners made of colored silk in the Buddha halls.
[Those of the lowest grade, even if unable to perform all these merits and virtues,
should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively recite Amitābha Buddha

. They rejoice, believe, and delight, and give rise to no doubt. With the utmost sincere mind they vow to be born in that land. When such a person is about to die, he dreams of that Buddha and likewise attains rebirth. His merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the middle grade.]

Those of the lowest grade (the lowest class): even if unable to perform all the merits and virtues described above, they should give rise to the mind of supreme bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively recite Amitābha Buddha. They rejoice, believe, and delight, and give rise to no doubt. With the utmost sincere mind they vow to be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss. When such a person is about to die, he dreams of Amitābha Buddha and likewise attains rebirth in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss. His merit, virtue, and wisdom are next to those of the middle grade.
The above three grades are those who practice the Pure Land exclusively; what follows explains those who do not practice the Pure Land exclusively.

[If there are sentient beings who dwell in the Great Vehicle, and with a pure mind turn toward Amitāyus, even to ten thoughts, vowing to be born in his land; and those who hear this profound Dharma and at once give rise to faith and understanding, even to obtaining a single thought of pure mind and, with that single thought, recollect that Buddha — such a person, at the time of death, as though in a dream, sees Amitābha Buddha and will certainly be born in that land, gaining non-retrogression and supreme bodhi.]

If there are sentient beings who dwell in the Great Vehicle and, with a pure mind (undefiled by deluded thoughts), invoke Amitābha Buddha, even to ten recitations at the point of death, vowing to be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss; and again, if there are sentient beings who hear the Pure Land Dharma-gate and at once give rise to faith and understanding, even to obtaining a single thought of pure mind and with that single thought invoking Amitābha Buddha — these two kinds of people, at the time of death, as though in a dream, see Amitābha Buddha and will certainly be born in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss, gaining the stage of non-retrogression and reaching Buddhahood.

[Moreover, Ānanda, if good men or good women hear this scripture, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, copy and make offerings to it, continuing day and night, and seek birth in that land; give rise to the bodhi mind, uphold all the precepts, firmly keeping them without violation; benefit sentient beings and give to them all the good roots they have made, bringing them peace and joy; and recollect Amitābha Buddha and his land — such a person, at the end of life, with the Buddha's form and marks and all manner of adornment, is born in the jeweled land, quickly hears the Dharma, and never falls back.]

Moreover, Ānanda, if good men or good women hear this scripture, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, copy and make offerings to it, and day and night without interruption seek birth in the Western land of Ultimate Bliss; give rise to the bodhi mind, uphold all the precepts, firmly keeping them without violation; benefit sentient beings and give to them all the good roots they have made, bringing them peace and joy; and recollect Amitābha Buddha and the land of Ultimate Bliss — such a person, at the end of life, with the Buddha's form and marks and all manner of adornment, is born in the jeweled land, quickly hears the Dharma, and never falls back.

[The precepts] Prohibiting the non-precept and guarding against evil. The precepts laid down by the Buddha are variously divided into the five precepts, the eight precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, and the full precepts. [With the Buddha's form and marks] Their form and marks are like the Buddha's — a body of true golden hue with the thirty-two marks.

[Moreover, Ānanda, if sentient beings wish to be born in that land, though they cannot greatly practice vigor and meditative concentration and fully uphold the sutras and precepts, they should at least do good. That is: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to speak frivolously; sixth, not to speak harshly; seventh, not to speak duplicitously; eighth, not to be greedy; ninth, not to be angry; tenth, not to be deluded. Thus, day and night they reflect upon the manifold merits and virtues and manifold adornments of Amitābha Buddha in the land of Ultimate Bliss. With single-minded hearts they take refuge, bow in homage, and make offerings. When such a person is about to die, without alarm or fear, with a mind not confused, he attains rebirth in that Buddha's land.]

Moreover, Ānanda, if sentient beings wish to be born in that land, though they cannot greatly practice vigor and meditative concentration and fully uphold the sutras and precepts, they should at least do good. That is: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely (not to speak words that are false and untrue); fifth, not to speak frivolously (not to speak filthy words, meaningless words, or words containing lewd intent); sixth, not to speak harshly (not to revile or mock others with vicious words); seventh, not to speak duplicitously (not to stir up trouble and set others at variance); eighth, not to be greedy; ninth, not to be angry; tenth, not to be deluded (not to be foolish). Thus, day and night they reflect upon the manifold merits and virtues and manifold adornments of Amitābha Buddha in the land of Ultimate Bliss. With single-minded hearts they take refuge, bow in homage, and make offerings. When such a person is about to die, without alarm or fear, with a mind not confused, he attains rebirth in that Buddha's land.

[If one has many affairs and cannot leave the household, and has no leisure to greatly cultivate the fasts and precepts and keep a single pure mind. When one has free time, rectify body and mind, cut off desire and put away anxiety, and with a compassionate mind be diligent. One should not be angry or envious, and must not be gluttonous
tiè
or stingy
qiān
and grudging. One must not later regret, nor be of two minds.]

If one's affairs are many and one cannot leave the household, and has no leisure to greatly cultivate the fasts and precepts and keep a single pure mind, then whenever one has free time, one should rectify body and mind, cut off desire and put away anxiety, and with a compassionate mind be diligent. One should not be angry or envious, and must not be gluttonous or stingy. Toward the Pure Land Dharma-gate one must not later regret, nor be of two minds.
[No leisure] To have no time; to be unable to manage it. [Gluttonous (tiè)] Insatiably greedy. [Later regret] Faith that is not firm, believing first and doubting afterward.

[One should be filial and obedient, sincere, loyal, and trustworthy. One should believe that the words of the Buddhist scriptures are profound, and believe that doing good brings blessings. Uphold and keep such teachings without fail. Reflect and ponder deeply, wishing to attain liberation. Day and night constantly recollect, wishing to be born in Amitābha Buddha's pure Buddha-land. Those who for ten days and ten nights, or even one day and one night, do not break off, at the end of life all attain rebirth in that land and practice the bodhisattva path.]

One should be filial and obedient, sincere, loyal, and trustworthy. One should believe that the words of the Buddhist scriptures are profound, and believe that doing good brings blessings. Uphold and keep such teachings without fail. Reflect and ponder deeply, wishing to attain liberation (to escape the round of rebirth). Day and night constantly recollect, wishing to be born in Amitābha Buddha's pure Buddha-land. Those who for ten days and ten nights, or even one day and one night, do not break off, at the end of life all attain rebirth in that land and practice the bodhisattva path.

[All those reborn there attain non-retrogression, are all endowed with the thirty-two marks of golden hue, and will all become Buddhas. In whatever direction's Buddha-land they wish to become Buddhas, it is according to the wish of their hearts. According to their diligence, sooner or later, seeking the Way without rest, they will certainly attain it, and will not lose what they have vowed.]

All those reborn there attain the stage of non-retrogression, are all endowed with the thirty-two marks of golden hue, and will all become Buddhas. In whatever direction's Buddha-land they wish to become Buddhas, it is entirely according to the wish of their hearts. According to their diligence, sooner or later, seeking the Way without rest, they will certainly become Buddhas, and will not lose what they have vowed.
[Ānanda, because of this benefit of meaning, the Tathāgatas of immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled, boundless worlds all together praise all the merit and virtue of Amitāyus Buddha.]
Ānanda, because of this benefit of meaning, the Tathāgatas of the immeasurable, countless, inconceivable, unequaled, boundless worlds all together praise all the merit and virtue of Amitābha Buddha.
[Benefit of meaning] “Meaning” is just and fitting principle and conduct; “benefit” is benefit and advantage.

blocks.text: 26. Paying Homage, Making Offerings, and Hearing the Dharma

inline.s: [Moreover, Ānanda, the assemblies of bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, wishing to behold and worship Amitāyus Buddha of the land of Ultimate Bliss, each with fragrant flowers, banners, and jeweled canopies, proceed to where the Buddha is. Reverently making offerings, they listen to and receive the sutras and Dharma, proclaim and spread the teaching, and praise the merit, virtue, and adornments of that Buddha-land.]

Moreover, Ānanda, the assemblies of bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, wishing to behold and worship Amitābha Buddha of the land of Ultimate Bliss, each with fragrant flowers, banners, and jeweled canopies, go to where Amitābha Buddha is. Reverently making offerings, they hear and receive the sutras and Dharma spoken by Amitābha Buddha, and again proclaim and spread his teaching throughout the ten directions, praising the merit and adornments of the land of Ultimate Bliss.
